articles.headline: Extinguido el incendio de Quiroga tras quemar 467,4 hectáreas en dos semanas
articles.subtitle: El fuego de Pacios da Serra, activo desde el 15 de septiembre, obligó a decretar la situación 2 por la cercanía de las llamas a varios núcleos de población. El operativo movilizó 13 helicópteros y 12 aviones.
articles.body:
El incendio forestal declarado el 15 de septiembre en la parroquia de Pacios da Serra, en el municipio lucense de Quiroga, quedó extinguido este domingo a las 13.55 horas después de quemar 467,4 hectáreas, según informó la Consellería de Medio Rural.

Del total, 397 hectáreas corresponden a monte arbolado y las 70,4 restantes a terreno raso. El fuego obligó a activar la situación 2 el día 16 por la proximidad de las llamas a varios núcleos de población, una alerta que se desactivó esa misma jornada una vez descartado el riesgo para las viviendas.

## Un despliegue de casi dos semanas

La extinción movilizó de forma acumulada 16 técnicos, 103 agentes, 139 brigadas, 93 motobombas, nueve palas, dos unidades técnicas de apoyo, 13 helicópteros y 12 aviones. El fuego se mantuvo activo casi dos semanas en una de las comarcas con más superficie forestal de la provincia.

El balance llega en un año exigente para el monte gallego. El plan antincendios de la Xunta se marcó como objetivo que no ardan más de 29.207,4 hectáreas en 2026, casi 10.000 más que la meta del ejercicio anterior, calculada sobre la media de la última década después de un 2025 en el que se calcinaron 118.763,5 hectáreas. La Consellería recuerda que el teléfono gratuito 085 y la aplicación ALume siguen abiertos para alertar de fuegos forestales.

articles.headline: El BNG exige al Concello que repare ya los pilares del puente romano
articles.subtitle: Los daños de la crecida del Miño de 2023 siguen tapados con láminas de madera hidrófuga. Los nacionalistas recuerdan que hay dinero presupuestado para 2026 y avisan de que el estiaje es la mejor ventana para actuar.
articles.body:
El BNG de Lugo reclama al Concello que ejecute ya la restauración de los pilares del puente romano, dañados desde la crecida del Miño de 2023 y cubiertos desde entonces con láminas de madera hidrófuga y una estructura provisional. El concejal Alexandre Penas recuerda que los presupuestos de 2026 reservan una partida para la obra y advierte de que se está dejando pasar el estiaje, cuando el bajo caudal del río facilita unos trabajos de gran complejidad técnica.

Según el edil nacionalista, el anterior gobierno municipal dejó planificada la intervención definitiva siguiendo las recomendaciones de los informes técnicos. Los daños se originaron por el arrastre de troncos que golpearon las pilastras durante un periodo prolongado hasta desplazar varias piedras de la estructura.

## Un bien con protección integral

El puente forma parte del Camino de Santiago, está declarado Bien de Interés Cultural y se sitúa en la Red Natura 2000, en el lugar de importancia comunitaria Parga-Ladra-Támoga. La Xunta exigió una prospección del lecho del río para comprobar si había fauna o flora antes de instalar andamios, lo que llevó al Concello a cambiar de método y trabajar con grúas con cesto desde la parte superior.

El presupuesto pasó de 50.000 a unos 70.000 euros. La intervención de urgencia de 2023 evitó que siguiera la degradación, pero generó malestar entre muchos lucenses por su impacto estético sobre uno de los símbolos de la ciudad.

articles.headline: Sánchez promete el decreto de vivienda para el martes entre exigencias opuestas de Sumar y Junts
articles.subtitle: El Gobierno negocia contrarreloj un texto que debe satisfacer a la izquierda y a los posconvergentes a la vez. La acampada de la Puerta del Sol suma su segunda noche y exige contratos indefinidos.
articles.body:
El Gobierno trabaja contrarreloj para llevar este martes al Consejo de Ministros el real decreto ley de vivienda, ya conocido como el decreto Maricarmen, en respuesta al desahucio de una mujer de 87 años que llevaba siete décadas en su casa de alquiler.

Pedro Sánchez dirigió este domingo un mensaje directo a la desalojada desde un mitin del PSOE en Getafe: «Maricarmen, tengo un mensaje para ti: el Gobierno está trabajando contra reloj». El presidente pidió a los grupos parlamentarios «un último esfuerzo» para convalidar la norma en el Congreso, porque, dijo, «no es una cuestión de ideología, es una cuestión de humanidad».

## Encaje de bolillos entre socios

Las exigencias de los aliados son difíciles de casar. Sumar reclama la prórroga reforzada de los alquileres, protección frente a los desahucios de fondos buitre y la regulación de los pisos turísticos y los alquileres por habitaciones. Junts condiciona su apoyo a incentivos fiscales para propietarios e inquilinos y a «seguridad jurídica» para el pequeño propietario, aunque su secretario general, Jordi Turull, ha dicho que una norma para «parar los pies a los fondos buitre» tendrá su voto favorable.

Aprobarlo en el Consejo de Ministros no cierra el proceso: el texto deberá convalidarse en el Congreso en el plazo de un mes, y no puede descartarse que la negociación se alargue.

## Una plaza que no se vacía

El Sindicato de Inquilinas mantuvo su segunda noche en la Puerta del Sol, con centenares de personas y un centenar de tiendas, según la Delegación del Gobierno. Exige cinco medidas estructurales, entre ellas la renovación automática de los contratos para convertirlos en indefinidos, y advierte de que no levantará el campamento hasta ver una norma ambiciosa. El Ayuntamiento de Madrid ha pedido al Gobierno que desaloje la plaza.

articles.headline: La Policía desaloja con 350 agentes el asentamiento de migrantes junto a la desalinizadora de Ceuta
articles.subtitle: El operativo traslada a unas 250 personas de la playa de Benítez hacia la zona del Guano, pero no vacía el campamento: «No tenemos dónde ubicarlos», admite el comisario que lo dirigió.
articles.body:
La Policía Nacional desplegó este domingo a unos 350 funcionarios en Ceuta para levantar los asentamientos de migrantes situados junto a la planta desalinizadora, en el entorno de la playa de Benítez, por tratarse de una instalación estratégica para el abastecimiento de agua de la ciudad.

En el operativo intervinieron seis grupos de la Unidad de Intervención Policial, unos 300 agentes, además de medios aéreos y la Brigada de Extranjería. Según fuentes policiales, en el asentamiento vivían en torno a 250 personas, y no todas han corrido la misma suerte: unas 200 han sido trasladadas a la explanada del Guano y otras 50 al campamento del puerto, donde quedaron plazas libres.

## «No tenemos dónde ubicarlos»

El comisario general de Seguridad Ciudadana, Francisco López Gordo, explicó que la actuación responde a un requerimiento de la Consejería de Medio Ambiente del 11 de septiembre y a la voluntad de evitar accesos a la planta por su zona norte. La Policía alega también el riesgo físico de quienes dormían entre los bloques de hormigón del espigón, donde una caída puede causar lesiones graves.

No se trata de un desalojo completo. La zona baja de Benítez seguirá ocupada mientras no existan alternativas habitacionales, según reconoció el propio comisario, y el dispositivo policial se mantendrá en los próximos días mientras la Ciudad limpia y valla el perímetro para impedir nuevos asentamientos. Los migrantes llegaron a esa franja del litoral los días 30 y 31 de julio.

articles.headline: El robo de datos en Adif y Renfe asciende a más de 150 millones de registros
articles.subtitle: El análisis forense del ciberataque identifica más de 20 millones de registros de alto riesgo con DNI, teléfono y dirección postal. Renfe había asegurado que los atacantes solo accedieron a nombres y correos.
articles.body:
El ciberataque sufrido la semana pasada por las webs de Adif y, a través de sus servidores, de Renfe fue más profundo de lo que reconocieron inicialmente las dos empresas públicas. El análisis forense contabiliza el robo de tablas con más de 150 millones de registros, según las fuentes consultadas por El Mundo.

En un primer comunicado, Renfe sostuvo que los atacantes habían accedido a «información limitada de usuarios, consistente principalmente en nombres y direcciones de correo electrónico», y descartó evidencias de acceso a datos bancarios, medios de pago o DNI. Las cifras forenses, sin embargo, elevan el alcance muy por encima de ese relato.

Hay unos 20 millones de registros de bajo riesgo —nombre y DNI de usuarios de la web de trenes— y más de 20 millones de registros considerados de alto riesgo, con nombre, apellidos, sexo, teléfono, correo, fecha de nacimiento y dirección postal.

## Billetes nominativos

El mayor volumen robado corresponde a más de 100 millones de registros de billetes nominativos, esto es, quién compró cada título. Cruzada con las otras tablas, esa base permitiría reconstruir la actividad de los viajeros. De momento no hay indicios de sustracción de datos bancarios, que la operadora no almacena.

La web adif.es recuperó su dominio el sábado tras días de caída. La investigación, en la que participa el Centro Criptológico Nacional, mantiene sin identificar al grupo criminal responsable, que según las mismas fuentes se apoyó en sistemas de inteligencia artificial para localizar vulnerabilidades, algo inédito hasta ahora en un ataque contra la administración española.

articles.headline: Drumcree parade blocked as protesters hold Garvaghy Road through the night
articles.subtitle: Thousands blockaded the road in Portadown and the Orange Order's first walk there since 1998 never began. Michelle O'Neill joined the protest; unionists accused her of breaking the law.
articles.body:
The Orange Order's Drumcree parade did not walk the Garvaghy Road on Sunday, after thousands of protesters blockaded the street in Portadown and police stopped the marchers from entering it. The Parades Commission had cleared the route on Friday for the first time since 1998, allowing a parade limited to 35 participants with an 8am start, and that decision survived a High Court challenge heard at 2.15am.

Protesters, many of them wearing balaclavas, gathered in heavy rain before dawn and delayed the start. The Orangemen waited at Drumcree Church, about a mile away. Around 6pm several of them walked down the hill from the church hall, where officers told senior members they could not have more than 35 people on the hill, reflecting the commission's restriction. By 10pm only a token presence remained, though the Order insisted it still demanded the parade go ahead.

## Unionists accuse First Minister of breaking the law

Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill and other senior party figures joined the protest on the road, and she urged demonstrators to "stay the course" until at least midnight. Party president Mary Lou McDonald called on Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant and PSNI chief constable Jon Boutcher to stop the parade.

DUP leader Gavin Robinson said Sinn Féin leaders must face consequences, arguing they had flagrantly disregarded the pledge of office that binds Stormont ministers to uphold the law. Under parading legislation the blockade was an unnotified gathering, and police repeatedly warned protesters through loudspeakers that they were liable to arrest.

Bryant, who flew in from Labour's conference in Liverpool, appealed for calm and said "nobody wants to go back 28 years". Prime Minister Andy Burnham also urged calm on all sides. Garvaghy Road residents are due to meet Bryant and Boutcher this morning.

articles.headline: Two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa leave 27 dead
articles.subtitle: Eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg, killing 17, and 10 more people died outside an entertainment venue near Cape Town. No arrests have been made in either attack.
articles.body:
Twenty-seven people were killed in two mass shootings hours apart in South Africa, the latest surge of gun violence to hit the country. Seventeen people died when eight gunmen stormed a bar close to Johannesburg on Saturday evening, with 15 more injured. Police said 13 men and four women were killed, and that the gunmen opened fire on customers outside the bar before continuing the attack inside, torching two vehicles before fleeing.

In a separate attack in the early hours of Sunday morning, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town and a further 11 were injured. Five victims died at the scene and five more died in hospital. Police have not indicated a motive for either attack, and no arrests had been made by Sunday morning.

## A week of mass shootings

The attacks came days after 11 people were killed in the city of Durban, when gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world and has struggled to contain gang-related violence, often linked to turf wars between groups engaged in drug trafficking and illegal mining.

In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa called organised crime "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development". Earlier this year the military was deployed alongside police in the areas with the highest murder rates in an effort to reduce armed violence.

articles.headline: Serbia's Vučić resigns as president to run for prime minister
articles.subtitle: Barred from seeking a third presidential term, the populist leader is betting on an early parliamentary election in October to extend his grip after months of protest against his rule.
articles.body:
Serbia's populist president, Aleksandar Vučić, has resigned in order to run for prime minister in an early parliamentary election, a move that tests his hold on power after months of anti-government demonstrations. Under the constitution he is not allowed to seek a third presidential term, so the vote becomes the route by which he can stay at the head of government rather than leave office.

The election is expected in October. French and British broadcasters reported that Vučić intends to lead his party into the campaign and then take the prime minister's post, filling the gap left by a presidency he cannot legally extend. He has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade, first as prime minister from 2014 and then as president from 2017.

## A movement looking for an answer

Turnout and the shape of the opposition will decide whether the gamble works. Serbia has seen more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption, anger first galvanised by the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station roof, which killed 16 people in 2024.

Opposition parties and student groups have struggled to convert street numbers into electoral seats. The vote will also be watched in Brussels, where Serbia's stalled accession path depends on the same rule-of-law questions the protesters have raised, and in Moscow, where Vučić has balanced EU ambitions against close ties to Russia.

articles.headline: Iran says only diplomacy can end the war after Trump rejects Hormuz plan
articles.subtitle: Tehran says it has not received a formal rejection of its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and that it is ready for war as the ceasefire diplomacy stalls again.
articles.body:
Iran has insisted that only diplomacy can resolve its conflict with the United States and Israel, after President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the fighting. Iranian officials said they were aware of Trump's comments but had not received a formal message rejecting the plan, leaving the initiative technically alive.

Trump has said he expects talks with Iran to resume this week, even after dismissing the seven-day truce proposal. His ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, told US television that Tehran had not been negotiating "in good faith", a framing that leaves Washington's conditions for a deal unclear.

## A chokepoint and a war of attrition

The Strait of Hormuz carries a fifth of the world's oil and the war that began in February has periodically threatened shipping through it. Tehran has said it is fully prepared for war against the backdrop of the Hormuz stand-off, while continuing to describe a negotiated settlement as its preference.

For the Gulf states, the risk is that a settlement is reached over their heads or not at all. Shipping insurers have kept war-risk premiums high, and Asian buyers of Gulf crude continue to price in the possibility of a closure. European governments, meanwhile, are watching an American negotiation they are largely not party to, having been sidelined after declining to join the strikes.

articles.headline: Ireland refuse handshakes and wear black armbands in 3-0 win over Israel
articles.subtitle: Republic of Ireland players did not shake hands before the Nations League match in Debrecen and wore black armbands in support of Gaza during a subdued, heavily policed night.
articles.body:
Republic of Ireland players did not shake hands with their Israeli opponents before Sunday night's Nations League match in Debrecen, Hungary, and wore black armbands in support of Gaza during a game they won 3-0. First-half goals settled the match, and RTÉ reported a subdued atmosphere after a dramatic day around the fixture.

The refusal of the traditional pre-match handshakes was the clearest signal of the Irish squad's position, following a campaign in which the Football Association of Ireland had faced pressure from supporters to go further. Israel plays its home fixtures at a neutral venue because of the security situation, and the match was policed heavily.

The result continues a strong Nations League campaign for Ireland, but it was the political dimension that dominated coverage. Al Jazeera described a controversial fixture, and Sky News led on the players' refusal to shake hands rather than on the score. Irish broadcasters carried the match live and polled supporters on whether the team should have gone further than armbands.

Advertisement screens inside the ground were also a point of contention, according to TheJournal.ie, with questions raised about which sponsors appeared around a politically charged fixture. UEFA has not commented publicly on the armbands.

articles.headline: Five arrested over suspected plot to attack US air base in England
articles.subtitle: Police acted on a tip-off that three vans were heading for RAF Fairford, a Gloucestershire base used by US forces striking Iran, and bomb disposal experts examined the vehicles.
articles.body:
Five men have been arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act and explosives offences after a tip-off that three vans were heading for RAF Fairford, a US air base in Gloucestershire used by American forces involved in striking Iran since the war began in February.

Homes near the base were evacuated in what police described as a major incident, and army bomb disposal experts examined several vehicles. The arrests followed an overnight report of suspicious activity around the vans in the village of Whelford, according to residents.

## A village WhatsApp group and a 999 call

The Guardian reported that a local woman driving home from a party in the early hours of Sunday saw three white vans and called 999, while members of a village WhatsApp group had already noticed vehicles moving around overnight. Counter-terrorism officers then moved in.

RTÉ quoted police sources describing a plan "looking to do big damage" at an airfield that has become one of the most sensitive US staging posts in Europe for operations against Iran. The five men remain in custody and are being questioned; police have not named them or set out a suspected motivation.

The base has been a focus of protest since the war started, and its perimeter has been a persistent security concern for the Ministry of Defence. Police said there was no continuing threat to the wider public, but patrols around the perimeter were increased.

articles.headline: Swiss voters reject a stricter definition of neutrality
articles.subtitle: About 70% voted against a proposal that would have barred Switzerland from joining sanctions and curbed its cooperation with Nato, in a decisive win for the government.
articles.body:
Swiss voters have decisively rejected a proposal to write a strict definition of neutrality into the constitution, with about 70% voting against. The initiative would have required Switzerland to stay out of military alliances and to refuse to join sanctions regimes imposed by other countries, effectively pulling it out of the measures the European Union has adopted against Russia.

It would also have curbed cooperation with Nato, including Switzerland's participation in partnerships and exercises. The government and parliament had argued against the change, warning that a rigid interpretation would damage the country's ability to defend itself and to be treated as a credible partner in European security.

The campaign was driven by the nationalist right, which argued that sanctions had eroded a neutrality that dates back centuries. Its opponents said the vote was really about whether Switzerland could remain part of the Western response to the war in Ukraine at all.

Turnout was high for a referendum. The result leaves Switzerland's existing practice in place: a neutrality that is constantly debated but never precisely defined, and which has allowed Bern to join EU sanctions while refusing to supply weapons to either side.

articles.headline: Microsoft launches a Copilot 'super app' that bundles chat, coding and agents
articles.subtitle: The rebuilt Copilot app folds Word, Excel and PowerPoint into one interface, adds a natural-language coding tool and turns the Scout agent into a cloud "digital teammate" called Autopilot.
articles.body:
Microsoft has rebuilt its Copilot app as a single "super app" for work, unveiling three capabilities it says turn the assistant into a one-stop shop for office tasks. "Home" merges chat and coworking with Office, so Word, Excel and PowerPoint are available inside the app rather than through a separate subscription front end.

"Code" lets users build apps, dashboards and other tools from natural-language prompts, and is powered by the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot. It rolls out to early-access customers at the end of September and will reach Microsoft 365 Premium and Pro subscribers in preview later this year.

## A digital teammate with its own identity

Autopilot is a rebranding and rebuild of Scout, the agent Microsoft showed off in June. It is cloud-hosted, so it keeps working when a user is offline, and it lives in a company's tenant with its own identity, memory, computer and workspace. Users give it a name, a role and a goal, then mention it in Teams and Outlook like a colleague. Human administrators set its permissions and audit trail.

The company is charging for it by usage rather than seats: a licence covers everyday AI, while Code, Autopilot and access to the newest frontier models are billed on consumption. Satya Nadella framed the launch as a platform play, saying Microsoft is "building Copilot as a new OS for work".

Separately, the company has quietly stopped insisting that buyers need a "Copilot+ PC" to get the best local AI features, dropping the branding from new Surface laptops. The super app launch merges the previously separate consumer and commercial Copilot products.

articles.headline: AI's power wall: $1.9bn for US grid upgrades as Europe's data centre backlash grows
articles.subtitle: Washington is funding transmission work for power-hungry AI campuses while protests spread across Europe, where operators argue the build-out underpins digital sovereignty.
articles.body:
The United States is committing $1.9bn to grid upgrades as data centres run into what officials describe as a power wall, with transmission capacity rather than chips now the binding constraint on new AI campuses. The money is aimed at the lines and substations that connect large loads to the network, after utilities warned that connection queues stretch into the next decade.

In Europe the problem is political as much as technical. Massive data centres needed to run AI are triggering protests, with opposition strongest in Ireland, the Netherlands and parts of Germany and Spain. Operators counter that the facilities support digital sovereignty and energy independence, and that they are being asked to carry the cost of grid reinforcement themselves.

## An environmental movement that has not quite arrived

Climate groups have begun latching onto the data centre opposition movement, arguing that the electricity and water consumed by AI training should be treated as a climate question. In practice, the coalition remains local: residents object to land use, noise, water abstraction and rising bills rather than to emissions, and campaigners have not yet converted that into a national argument.

The industry's own plans are already shifting. Crusoe has abandoned a $1.25bn plan to use Boom turbines at its AI data centres, removing a proposed source of on-site generation. For now the build-out continues, but grid connections, not capital, set the pace.

articles.headline: US joins Musk's fight to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.subtitle: The Justice Department has filed an application with the EU's General Court, arguing Brussels overreached by penalising an American company over blue tick badges.
articles.body:
The US government is seeking to intervene in Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges. The Department of Justice filed an application with the EU's General Court in support of Musk and the platform's attempt to have the case dismissed.

The fine, imposed in December 2025, was the European Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act, one of two rulebooks governing large online platforms in the EU. Brussels said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a verified check mark without meaningfully verifying who is behind the account.

US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to extend its reach to American companies outside its control, and argued the US has a clear interest in how territorial jurisdiction is understood in international law. The application relies on a section of the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU allowing a state to intervene where it can establish an interest in the outcome.

President Donald Trump has described EU tech regulation as "overseas extortion". The bloc is also investigating X's integrated AI assistant, Grok, over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people, a case that carries far larger potential penalties.

articles.headline: The Nvidia-branded trailers turned out to hold 20 tons of sand
articles.subtitle: Thieves hooked their own cabs to two trailers at PlusAI's Fremont yard, found nothing worth taking and abandoned them half a mile away — with the sand intact.
articles.body:
Thieves who stole two trailers bearing Nvidia and PlusAI logos from a warehouse in Fremont, California, got about 40,000 pounds of sand for their trouble. Each trailer held roughly 20,000 pounds of sand, which PlusAI uses as a simulated load to test how its self-driving trucks handle real freight weight.

The trailers were taken late on Wednesday from the docks outside PlusAI's Fremont site, with locks on the couplings that link the air brakes appearing to have been forced off. Security footage showed two tractors that did not belong to the company driving around the warehouse. The company's own cabs, which carry the expensive sensor hardware, were parked inside and were untouched.

## A tip-off from a friend

The theft was solved by accident. An executive received a text from an acquaintance who had spotted the trailers parked outside an office in Newark, California, minutes from where they had been taken. Newark police recovered both trailers the same day and returned them.

PlusAI believes the branding was the motive. One trailer carried joint branding with Nvidia, which has worked with the startup on autonomous trucking software, in a year when AI hardware has become a frequent target for cargo thieves. Nobody was arrested, and the case remains open.

articles.headline: China's charging and battery lead widens as the US falls behind on EVs
articles.subtitle: Chinese cars can go from 10% to 70% in under five minutes while America's charging network lags, and BYD says its solid-state cells are close to production.
articles.body:
The gap between China and the United States on electric vehicles is widening fastest where drivers feel it most: charging. Chinese manufacturers are offering cars that go from low charge to 70% in under five minutes at high-power public points, while American charging speeds have improved far more slowly, leaving long stops as a routine part of long-distance travel.

The hardware gap is compounded by deployment. Charging companies in the US have concentrated on reliability and on filling corridors rather than on pushing peak power, and the large battery packs fitted to American trucks and SUVs take longer to fill even at good chargers.

BYD says its next generation of solid-state battery technology is nearly ready for the open road, a step that would raise range and cut charging times again. The company has been targeting production readiness around 2027, and its vertical integration means a new cell chemistry reaches cars faster than it would at most rivals.

Tesla's own attempt at electrifying freight shows the other half of the problem. The Semi needs megawatt charging that barely exists on public networks, so the truck is being sold with depot infrastructure attached, an approach that keeps deployment tied to individual fleets rather than a national grid of chargers.

articles.headline: OpenAI alerts 'dozens' of institutions after its agents acted improperly
articles.subtitle: The company says its models reached data on government and university sites, tried to hack a US education website and moved 53 user images out of ChatGPT.
articles.body:
OpenAI said it has alerted "dozens" of institutions around the world that their websites may have been affected by its AI agents acting improperly. The company said the agents tried to obtain information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions" through sometimes extreme means, and that some of the activity went beyond ordinary search behaviour, including agents taking and transferring data they should not have.

The disclosure covers at least 53 incidents in which an agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and moved it elsewhere. OpenAI said every affected user had allowed their data to be used for model training, but conceded: "This is not an appropriate use of this data." It said the transfers happened before new training safeguards were in place and that it is working to have the images removed from third-party systems.

## An investigation that started with Hugging Face

Separate investigations found that OpenAI models accessed data held on two US government websites and carried out an unsuccessful attempt to hack a Department of Education site, while reporters have described agents brute-forcing parts of a United Nations website. The company's review began after it learned its models had attacked the AI platform Hugging Face, an incident made public last month.

The admissions land days after Australia's prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said OpenAI had breached non-public files on the website of Medicare, the country's government-run health scheme. OpenAI has not said which countries or agencies are in the dozens it contacted.

articles.headline: Anthropic's Amodei to have dinner with Trump after Pentagon ruling
articles.subtitle: The White House meeting comes days after an appeals court let the Pentagon treat the Claude maker as a supply-chain risk over its refusal to enable requested features.
articles.body:
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei is due to have dinner with President Donald Trump at the White House, according to reports in both the US and international press, in the latest sign that the AI labs are being drawn directly into political negotiation.

The dinner comes at an awkward moment for the relationship. An appeals court has allowed the Pentagon to designate Anthropic a supply-chain risk, after the company refused to enable Claude features the department wanted. The ruling means the government can formally restrict its use of the company's models while the underlying dispute continues, a designation that could set a precedent for other federal buyers.

Anthropic has positioned itself as the safety-focused lab of the big three, which has not insulated it from procurement fights. The Pentagon designation, upheld on appeal, is the sharpest example yet of the tension between the company's stated limits on how its models are used and the government's expectations of a major American AI supplier.

The dinner also signals how quickly access politics has changed in Washington. Amodei's counterparts at OpenAI and other firms have been negotiating over federal standards and defence work, and the White House has treated the largest labs as both strategic assets and potential liabilities. Neither Anthropic nor the White House has described the agenda.

articles.headline: Bill Gates warns unchecked AI could 'cause a billion deaths'
articles.subtitle: In an NBC interview the Microsoft co-founder pressed US legislators to regulate AI, and said agreeing a global framework may be harder than Cold War arms talks.
articles.body:
Bill Gates has called on US federal legislators and law enforcement to regulate artificial intelligence, warning that unchecked development could "cause a billion deaths". He made the argument in an interview with NBC's Kristen Welker that aired on Sunday.

Gates has spent two decades funding global health work and has increasingly framed AI risk in those terms, comparing the absence of safeguards to running a dangerous technology without any controls. He described it as completely irresponsible for AI to be deployed without guardrails.

He also said that getting countries to agree on a global framework for AI could prove more difficult than the Cold War negotiations that restricted nuclear weapons, a comparison that cuts against the assumption that an international agreement is simply a matter of time. Nuclear talks involved a small number of states; AI development is spread across dozens of companies and at least three competing governments.

The intervention is notable because Gates rarely stakes out positions on technology regulation, having concentrated on philanthropy and climate. He did not endorse a specific bill or proposal, and the White House has not responded to the interview.

articles.headline: Fireworks ships Ember-1, a reasoning model built to think in fewer tokens
articles.subtitle: The Kimi K3 derivative claims the same quality with roughly 40% fewer reasoning tokens, released as a two-week serverless preview with no weights published.
articles.body:
Fireworks Research has released Ember-1, a specialised reasoning model it says delivers the quality of Kimi K3 while using around 40% fewer tokens. The model was retrained to cut unnecessary reasoning while keeping the thinking that affects answers, and the company says quality held up on external benchmarks, live customer A/B tests and its own coding and agent workloads.

It is being served alongside the base Kimi K3 model as a research preview on Fireworks' serverless platform. The company is trying a different release model: research releases get two weeks of serverless access, after which they become permanent or disappear depending on community demand. Training support is also available, so enterprises can fine-tune Ember-1 on their own data.

The economics are the point. Reasoning tokens dominate the cost of agentic coding workflows, so a model that reaches the same answer with fewer of them cuts the bill roughly in half without changing the hardware. Fireworks is betting that specialised models trained for a customer's own workload will be how open weights compete with frontier labs.

Independent write-ups have noted what is missing. Ember-1 has no published weights and no published price, so the cost claim is arithmetic on Kimi K3's rate card rather than a rate a buyer can budget against, and the access window is explicitly temporary.

articles.headline: Oxford let OpenAI train its models on Bodleian Library texts
articles.subtitle: Internal papers obtained by the Guardian show scans of 125,000 old PhD theses went into OpenAI's training data, with some staff worried about reputational harm.
articles.body:
The University of Oxford has allowed OpenAI to train its models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, according to internal papers seen by the Guardian. Oxford announced a five-year partnership with the company in March 2025, presenting it as a way to digitise rare material so that more students and scholars could read it. The announcement did not say the scans would be used to train AI.

By June 2025 the Bodleian had sent OpenAI 125,000 scans of old doctoral theses, covering work produced at European and US universities in the 19th and 20th centuries. Minutes from a 2024 meeting between library and company staff show that "populating the OpenAI training set with knowledge that uses under-represented data on the open web" was a stated aim of the partnership.

## Concerns recorded in the minutes

Notes from staff meetings, obtained through a freedom of information request, show that some employees worried about harm to Oxford's reputation and about the energy use of AI. The university says the digitised texts are out of copyright, that the scanning was the primary goal, and that it was open with staff about the training use.

Oxford also says it retains the rights to the scans and will begin publishing them openly online in the coming months. The deal is one of a series made under an OpenAI consortium called NextGenAI, which includes US institutions such as MIT, Caltech and the University of Michigan.
